A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LEDOM and Reverse Reward study. All 20 pages of v2 and 21 pages of v3, including Appendices A–D, provide readable and matchable text, equations, tables, figures and algorithms.

before.justification: v2 reports original model-training curves, general benchmark results in Table 5, mathematical reasoning evaluations in Table 3, and generated case studies.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results, with general benchmarks in Table 3, mathematical reasoning evaluations in Table 4, and training curves and case studies in the appendices.

M1.justification: The reverse-token training objective, 2B/7B architectures, bidirectional reward, response reranking and step-level beam search are retained, including Algorithm 1. The new verification terminology and theoretical rationale do not change the proposed procedures.

E1.justification: Both use the same general/math/code pretraining corpus, OpenMathInstruct-2 fine-tuning data, general benchmark suite and four mathematical reasoning benchmarks. The behavioral task examples are also retained. Moving the general benchmark table into the main text adds no coverage.

E2.justification: The compared models and result-table rows remain the same, but Section 6.1 revises Best-of-N (Random)'s documented selection rule from choosing the best-scoring candidate in v2 to uniform random selection in v3. This changes the reported comparator definition; an implementation change or rerun is not established.

E3.justification: v3 Table 4 and Section 6.5 specify 64 Best-of-N candidates, whereas v2 Appendix D.2.3 specifies 4. v3 retains that appendix's value of 4, creating an inconsistent reported budget revision. The actual budget and any rerunning remain unresolved; other stated experimental settings are retained.

E4.justification: The sampling-size study, training-loss curves and behavioral and mathematical case studies are retained. v3 reinterprets existing evidence and discusses the existing AIME beam-search failure, without adding an ablation, robustness test or quantitative posterior-score analysis.

E5.justification: Both specify fine-tuning seed 0 in Appendix D.2.2. Neither adds repeated-run estimates, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests for the benchmark results.

E6.justification: Matched table entries, plotted values and case outputs are unchanged. Section 6.2 changes the stated baseline range from 43.0–95.6% to 42.0–95.6%, although v3 incorrectly describes this as a GSM8K range; 42.0 is the MATH-500 score. Section 6.3 and Figure 3 also newly describe improvement as monotonic, despite decreases in the retained plot.

T1.justification: Beyond v2's existing factorization, loss and reward formulas, v3 introduces Bayesian and conditional-entropy arguments in Sections 2.2–2.5, derives the noisy-channel scoring expression in Equation 8, and adds a posterior-degradation assumption, Proposition 1 and its proof in Section 5.1.

C1.justification: v3 makes noisy-channel verification and a claimed proof penalizing hallucinated reasoning central contributions. It shifts emphasis from foundation-model viability toward directional complementarity and elevates tentative reversal-curse observations into claims of natural resolution.

C2.justification: v3 adds entropy/capacity and posterior-reconstruction explanations and interprets retained results as validating posterior degradation. It explains OpenMath2's existing AIME beam-search failure and adds limitations concerning posterior approximation under distribution shift and missing learned-verifier comparisons. Explicit English-language and unsettled-training-recipe limitations are removed.

D1.justification: Section 5.1 explicitly documents the reversed scoring concatenation, and Section 6.5 adds inference-cost accounting. Hardware, training durations, hyperparameters and fine-tuning instructions remain unchanged in Appendices A/D. The new claim of only k beam evaluations per step conflicts with Algorithm 1's scoring of nk expanded candidates.

R1.justification: v3 grounds Reverse Reward in newly cited noisy-channel work by Shannon, Yu and Yee, and explicitly credits Varun et al.'s TRLM as inspiration for posterior reranking, positioning its extension around formal analysis and step-level verification. It also adds ELECTRA and removes Bhagavatula et al. This substantially revises contribution positioning.

P1.justification: The title becomes LEDOM: Reverse Language Model. The abstract, introduction and most main-text sections are extensively rewritten around posterior verification, with new theoretical subsections, condensed behavioral discussion, reorganized related work and headed limitations. The appendices largely retain their wording.

P2.justification: v2's Appendix Table 5 moves into Section 4 as v3 Table 3, with selective bolding and an expanded caption. Several other captions change and existing displays reflow, but the diagrams, plots, table structures and case-study panels are retained; no new figure or table is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 improves organization, prior-work attribution and discussion of beam-search limitations, but introduces reliability problems into its newly central theoretical claims. Proposition 1's approximate-equality assumption does not guarantee the ranking for every positive reward weight, and unchanged Table 7 supplies no likelihood comparisons supporting the asserted verification. The conflicting 64-versus-4 candidate budgets and Figure 3's unsupported monotonicity claim further weaken reporting. With empirical tables unchanged, these problems outweigh the presentation and qualification gains.
